name: Hana Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Hana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to any of it. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head stockperson at Greyfield Farm, so my day starts at half five with the cattle. We've got 160 suckler cows, which means cows that raise their own calves for beef, plus about 300 hectares of barley, oats and wheat. I check the calving pens, sort feed with Joel, then it's fencing, foot trimming, whatever's broken. I still keep the herd records in a green notebook in my coat pocket, and I'll be honest, I like it that way.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing every cow by her ways, which ones kick, which ones calve at night. What wears me out is the money and the owners. Greyfield was bought two years ago by an investment fund, Ardent Land, and the manager who answers to them lives three hours away and runs us by spreadsheet. My partner Tomas and I live in the farm cottage, and the rent comes straight out of my wage, so the job and the roof are the same thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hype, then. I'd believe that, to be fair, because most of what gets sold to farms is hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say at the union branch: told you so. The fund spent money on a herd app and a drone last year and neither one calved a cow. I'd post something short and a bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, it means my life stays the same, and my life is already tight. I earn less than a stockperson should, I've got about three weeks of money in the bank, and Ardent could sell Greyfield whenever the numbers suit them. AI going nowhere doesn't fix any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and push the union branch to fight the cottage deduction, because that's what's eating my pay. Tomas and I would keep cutting back, so no holiday again and the car stays patched. Over the year I'd try to get the branch to back a claim for a proper pay scale for senior stock staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Flat, really. Relieved the robots aren't coming, but not happy, because the things that keep me awake aren't machines. They're the rent line on my payslip and a fund I've never met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the robots stay away, what is the thing that would most likely end your time at Greyfield?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ardent selling up. If a new owner comes in and wants their own people, I lose the job and the cottage in the same month. I live in a cottage the farm owns, so if the job goes, my kitchen goes with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned three weeks of money. What gets cut first if something goes wrong, say the car breaks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car can't go, because the nearest other farm work is forty minutes' drive. So it'd be food first, cheaper everything, and Tomas would pick up extra bus runs. We've done it before, the winter the boiler died.

say: I'd tell the **union branch** that the farm tech was always hype and the herd app never calved a cow.
I'd post something short and a bit **smug** online about being proved right.
think: My life stays the same, and that life is already **tight** with three weeks of savings.
The real threat is **Ardent selling** Greyfield, because my job and my cottage would go together.
do: Push the union branch to fight the **cottage deduction** that comes out of her wage.
Cut household spending again, with **no holiday** and the car kept running on repairs.
Back a branch claim for a **pay scale** for senior stock staff within the year.
feel: **Relieved** the robots aren't coming, but flat, because her worries are rent and owners, not machines.
S0.quote: I live in a cottage the farm owns, so if the job goes, my kitchen goes with it.
fieldNote: Her **tied cottage** is the centre of everything: losing the job means losing the home.
She blames the **investment fund**, not technology, for low pay and insecurity.
Her job looks safe in this picture, but the **thin cushion** keeps money on her mind.

steps.text: Keep running the 160 suckler cows the same way, notebook and all
Get the union branch to challenge the cottage rent taken from her wage
Skip the holiday and keep patching the old car instead of replacing it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one sounds more like what's actually happening. The fund's already talking about it like it's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the cows don't care about software, and that'd get a laugh from Pete, our tractor driver. To the union I'd say this is exactly when we need to be organised, before they start not replacing people. Online I'd stay quiet, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the thinking part of my job is small, so AI writing plans doesn't touch me much. What scares me is the manager using AI to do the planning and ordering and then deciding one senior person who loves the app is better value than me. I won't use the thing, and they know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the union to push for a written agreement that nobody leaves without a proper talk and a notice period. When Pete retires next year, I'd fight to get him replaced, not swapped for a feed robot. And I'd try to put away fifty a month, which is all we've got spare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy turning into worried. It's like hearing a storm on the radio when you've got hay down. You know it's coming, you just don't know how bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't use the app. If the manager made it part of your job, what would you actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably let Joel do the typing and I'd tell him what to put in, which is what happens now. Joel's twenty-two and fast on a phone. I know that's not a long-term answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Greyfield would you worry about most in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pete, because he's sixty-one and doesn't have a pension worth naming. And Joel, oddly, because if they bring in robots slowly, the young lad is the cheapest one to let go first. The fund doesn't keep people out of kindness.

say: I'd tell the yard that **cows don't care** about software.
I'd tell the union this is the moment to **get organised**, before jobs quietly go unreplaced.
think: AI planning and ordering leaves my **hands-on work** mostly alone.
The manager might decide an **app-loving** senior hire is better value than me.
do: Push for a written **notice agreement** through the union before any job is cut.
Fight to have Pete **replaced by a person** when he retires next year.
Save **fifty a month**, which is all the household can spare.
feel: **Uneasy** turning into worried, like hearing a storm forecast with hay on the ground.
S1.quote: The fund doesn't keep people out of kindness.
fieldNote: She sees AI as a **management tool** that weakens her position, not as a threat to her hands.
Her refusal to use the herd app is a **real weak spot**, and she knows it.
Her worry quickly turns to **workmates**, Pete and Joel, before herself.

steps.text: Ask the union for a written notice agreement covering Greyfield staff
Argue for hiring a new tractor driver when Pete retires
Keep doing herd work by hand while Joel types records into the app
Put fifty a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's two lambing seasons from now, which is nothing on a farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this needs laws, fast, and I'd mean it. I'd be at every union meeting saying the companies selling this should pay for the people it replaces. I'd probably post more than I ever have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think Ardent would be first in the queue. A fund that runs a farm from a spreadsheet will buy a robot herd the day it's cheaper than me. The AI would do the manager's planning by 2028, and by 2031 the robots could do my calving checks and fencing, and I've got no savings to see me through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd get the union to demand a deal on redundancy pay and housing for anyone in a tied cottage. Tomas and I would ask his mum about moving into her spare room in town, just as a plan. In the year AGI lands, I'd stay put and work as hard as ever, because the robots aren't there yet and I need every payslip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. I think about the calving pen at three in the morning, which is my favourite place on earth, and a machine standing in it. And I'd be twenty-nine, with a degree and no money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap between the thinking AI and the robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep my job a bit longer than the office folk, but I watch it coming. Those three years I'd be working next to a clock. I'd rather have the time than not, but it's a strange kind of gift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move in with Tomas's mum. How would that conversation go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly at first. Tomas's mum, Ilse, is lovely, but she has a two-bedroom flat and a lot of opinions. I'd have to tell her that I, the one with the farming degree, can't keep a roof over us.

say: I'd say this needs **laws, fast**, and the tech companies should pay for the people they replace.
I'd turn up at **every union meeting** and post more than I ever have.
think: **Ardent** would buy a robot herd the day it's cheaper than paying me.
By **2031** robots could do my calving and fencing, and I've **no savings** to bridge it.
do: Push the union for **redundancy pay** and housing help for tied-cottage workers.
Ask Tomas's mother about **moving in** with her in town as a backup plan.
Keep working every shift until the robots arrive, to bank **every payslip**.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of a machine in the calving pen she loves.
**Ashamed** at needing family help despite her farming degree.
S2.quote: A fund that runs a farm from a spreadsheet will buy a robot herd the day it's cheaper than me.
fieldNote: She treats the **three-year gap** as a countdown rather than a chance to change course.
Her plans are **collective and defensive**: laws, union deals, family support.
Moving in with Tomas's mother brings real **shame** for someone proud of her skill.

steps.text: Press the union for redundancy pay and housing for tied-cottage workers
Campaign for laws making tech companies fund displaced farm workers
Ask Tomas's mother if they can move into her spare room

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years for the thinking side, eight for the robots. Better than two, still not much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as with the fast one: rules first, robots second. I'd tell people at the market that we've got a few years to make sure farm workers aren't the ones who pay for this. Out loud I'd sound calmer than I feel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Really, I think five years just means a slower walk to the same place. Ardent would bring in the planning AI by 2031, and by 2034 they'd have the robot feeders and the calving cameras. I'd be thirty-five with no house and no savings, and that's alarming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first years to look for a job on a small family farm, somewhere the owner can't afford robots. I'd ask around at the cattle market in Stenford, where everyone knows everyone. And I'd stay on the union branch committee to push for a law on retraining money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Not panic, but heavy. It's the feeling of knowing you'll have to leave somewhere you love, and having no say in when.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you avoid new technology. With five years' warning, would you learn to work with the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to say yes, but I don't think I would, not properly. I've never even used one of those chat AI things. I'd rather find the last farm that still wants a person who knows cows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the small family farm doesn't work out, what's the next option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I don't know, and I'm not going to pretend I do. Maybe the council's parks department, maybe a feed merchant. Tomas would say I'd go mad indoors, and he'd be right.

say: I'd tell people **rules first, robots second**, and that we have a few years to protect workers.
I'd sound **calmer** out loud than I feel inside.
think: Five years is a **slower walk** to the same place.
By **2034** I'd be thirty-five with no house and no savings.
do: Look for work on a **small family farm** that can't afford robots.
Ask around at the **Stenford cattle market** for openings.
Stay on the union committee to push for **retraining money** by law.
feel: **Heavy**, knowing she'll have to leave a place she loves with no say in when.
S3.quote: I'd rather find the last farm that still wants a person who knows cows.
fieldNote: Extra time doesn't change her **strategy**; she looks for a place to hide from the robots.
She openly admits she **wouldn't learn** to work with the machines.
Her fallback plans are **vague**, and she says so honestly.

steps.text: Ask at the Stenford cattle market for jobs on small family farms
Stay on the union branch committee through the change
Push for a law that funds retraining for farm workers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven when the thinking AI arrives and forty when the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so there's no excuse for governments not to get ready. I'd say it at the union and I'd say it to anyone who'd listen. I might even stand for the branch secretary job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years makes it a different story. I'd have time to save, and maybe time for the union to win something. I still think Greyfield's robots come the minute they're cheap, but by then I might not be at Greyfield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving properly, even a hundred a month, and pay off the car. I'd go for branch secretary so I'm at the table when deals get made. Somewhere in the first few years I'd start looking for a farm job with a house that isn't tied to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but it's a worry I can work with. It's like a long forecast. You can plan your cutting around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said Greyfield's owners will buy robots when they're cheap. Would you ever want to own a robot yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that sounds stubborn, and it is. I didn't train for four years to babysit a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas about the next ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomas we need to stop living in houses that come with jobs. That's the one thing ten years would let us fix. Everything else is out of our hands.

say: I'd say a decade leaves governments **no excuse** not to be ready.
I'd consider running for **branch secretary** of the union.
think: Ten years gives me time to **save** and for the union to win something.
By the time the robots arrive, I might **not be at Greyfield**.
do: Save **a hundred a month** and pay off the car.
Stand for **branch secretary** to be at the table for deals.
Look for a farm job where the **house isn't tied** to the work.
feel: **Worried**, but able to plan around it, like a long weather forecast.
S4.quote: I didn't train for four years to babysit a machine.
fieldNote: With ten years she shifts from **defence to planning**, mostly around housing.
Her **pride in skill** makes her reject any role managing robots.
The **tied cottage** stays her clearest risk in every scenario.

steps.text: Save a hundred a month and clear the car loan
Find a farm job that doesn't come with a tied cottage

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question, because there's no time and I've got no money. What would help is simple: if the job goes, the house shouldn't go with it. Tied-cottage workers need the right to stay a year, and there needs to be proper redundancy money paid by the people making the robots.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the land, and that's the whole story. If Greyfield belonged to a family, or to us, I'd feel very different about all of this. Robots aren't the problem on their own; it's who gets to decide when they come.

headlineQuote: Robots aren't the problem on their own; it's who gets to decide when they come.
portrait: Hana is a 27-year-old **head stockperson** on a fund-owned mixed farm, living with Tomas in a **tied cottage**.
She earns little, has about **three weeks** of savings, and keeps herd records in a paper notebook.
She is a committed **union member** who blames owners, not technology, for her insecurity.
She refuses to learn the farm's apps and would rather **find a small farm** than work with robots.
Her mood moves from uneasy to **alarmed** as the warning time shrinks.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time and no money to cushion losing both job and home.
whatWouldHelp: A right for **tied-cottage** workers to stay a year after losing the job.
**Redundancy money** paid for by the companies that make the robots.
